title: Bitter Cordial at Evensong
story: Dorothy Pruett steamed open a letter and learned that the innkeeper's 'late' husband is alive, so she began charging Ada Finch for her silence. On Thursday night Ada took a flask of hot blackcurrant cordial to the vestry, where Dorothy was working late on the parish accounts, and the cordial was laced with the inn's vermin powder.

setting.name: Bellweather
setting.summary: A small English village: a square, a manor with its greenhouse and boathouse on the river, an inn, the church vestry, a doctor's surgery, a post office, a railway halt and a disused mill. Someone is dead; the investigation begins the next morning.

rules.text: Strychnine is intensely bitter and brings on convulsions within fifteen to thirty minutes of being swallowed.

people.name: Clara Vale
people.voice: Composed, dry and exact; she chooses words like a woman choosing gloves. Polite to the point of chill with strangers, warmer once she respects you.
people.public: Edmund’s younger sister. She has run Vale Manor’s household for years and guards its privacy.

people.name: Silas Voss
people.voice: Measured, formal and faintly amused; speaks in tidy clauses and likes a Latin tag. Never rambles.
people.public: A precise, courteous solicitor who keeps an office in the vestry and handles the affairs of half the parish.

people.name: Ada Finch
people.voice: Warm, chatty and colloquial; calls people "love", runs on a little, and enjoys a bit of news more than she should.
people.public: Proprietor of the Rook & Lantern. She knows everyone’s habits and most of their business.

people.name: Dr Iris Marsh
people.voice: Clinical and direct, with brisk warmth underneath; says exactly what she observed and no more.
people.public: The village doctor. Methodical and direct; she is called whenever anyone in Bellweather is hurt or ill.

people.name: Arthur Bell
people.voice: A gruff country constable: terse, dry and matter-of-fact, with a soft spot he hides badly.
people.public: The village constable. He has secured the scene and asked you to investigate; he will hear an accusation when you can back it with evidence.

people.name: Edmund Vale
people.voice: Loud, confident and used to being obeyed; bluff good humour that turns cold when crossed.
people.public: Master of Vale Manor: a man of fixed habits, generous in public and hard in private.

people.name: The Reverend Thomas Hale
people.voice: Gentle and rambling, with a scholar’s digressions and a surprising steel when conscience is touched.
people.public: Vicar of St. Alden’s these twenty years. Gentle, absent-minded, and trusted with more secrets than anyone in the parish.

people.name: Dorothy Pruett
people.voice: Brisk, prim and precise, with relish for procedure and a keen, disapproving memory for other people’s business.
people.public: The postmistress. Every letter, parcel and telegram in Bellweather passes over her counter, and she forgets nothing.

people.name: Hugo Vale
people.voice: Quick, flippant and charming, full of London slang; hides nerves behind jokes and talks a little too fast.
people.public: Edmund’s nephew, down from London by train. Charming, restless and plainly bored by the country.

objects.name: Enamel flask
objects.desc: A blue enamel flask that had held hot blackcurrant cordial, found by the account ledgers in the vestry.

objects.name: Tin of vermin powder
objects.desc: A tin of strychnine-based rat powder kept on a shelf in the Rook & Lantern's cellar.

objects.name: Parish account ledgers
objects.desc: The parish ledgers Miss Pruett was writing up at the vestry table.

objects.name: Thursday menu card
objects.desc: A manor dinner menu card with pencilled times scribbled on the back.

objects.name: Dorothy's key ring
objects.desc: Miss Pruett's ring of keys, including a small brass key to the post office's registered-mail safe.

objects.name: Black pocket notebook
objects.desc: Dorothy's private notebook of monthly payments, kept in the registered-mail safe.

objects.name: Cellar teaspoon
objects.desc: A teaspoon left in the tin of vermin powder in the Rook & Lantern's cellar.

objects.name: Charred letter fragment
objects.desc: The unburnt corner of a moneylender's letter, left in the ash of the morning-room grate at Vale Manor.

objects.name: Grey hooded cloak
objects.desc: Clara Vale's grey church cloak, left on the Rook & Lantern's passage hooks after the harvest supper.

objects.name: Sealed tin of vermin powder
objects.desc: An unopened spare tin of strychnine rat powder from the inn's stores, set on the cellar shelf.

attitudes.content: From a steamed-open Liverpool letter: Ada Finch's husband is alive, so she is no widow.
Five pounds a month from Ada Finch for keeping quiet.
To finish the parish accounts in the vestry on Thursday night.
Dorothy Pruett is blackmailing her over her living husband.
Losing the inn's licence and her good name if the truth about her marriage gets out.
To silence her blackmailer with poisoned cordial while Dorothy works alone in the vestry.
To say she never left the bar all evening.
Dorothy spreading gossip about Edmund's debts, which she has read in letters to the manor.
To keep house and host the dinner at the manor.
Dorothy reporting the irregular client money orders she has noticed passing through her counter.
To go over Edmund Vale's new will with him at dinner.
To finish his correspondence in the vestry office before dinner.
Angry that Dorothy reads parish letters that pass through her hands.
To prepare Sunday's sermon in the vestry.
To play his Thursday game of chess with Dr Marsh.
To lock up the vestry for the night.
To play her Thursday chess game with the vicar.
To answer any call for a doctor.
To walk his evening round of the square.
To attend and secure any scene of sudden death.
To dine at home and settle his will with Voss.
To sit through dinner at the manor to stay in his uncle's good books.
To keep the bar as she always does.
To close up the post office and balance the day's takings.
To keep last night's dinner and the business of Edmund's will out of village talk.
To humour his sister and tell outsiders nothing about Thursday's dinner, unless his pride is pricked.
Bored stiff by Voss's talk of codicils, so he keeps a joking score of the time on his menu card.
To say as little as he can about the will dinner, so he doesn't cross Aunt Clara or lose his uncle's favour.
To keep her notebook of Ada's payments and the steamed Liverpool letter locked in the registered-mail safe, where only she has a key.
Rushed. The darts crowd will miss her if she is long, so she leaves the spoon in the tin and means to deal with it later.
To burn the London moneylender's demands for Edmund's debts before any policeman searches the manor, so the village never learns of them.
Village talk about how late the vicar stays at her surgery on Thursday nights, so she stays vague about the hours.
To record Thursday's game in the chess score-book as he always does, with its start and end times, as a scholar would.
To wear Miss Vale's grey hooded cloak from the passage hooks, so that anyone who sees her in the dark takes her for Clara Vale, whom Dorothy gossiped about.
The hooded woman in the grey cloak on the square was Miss Vale, because it was her church cloak.
Aunt Clara finding his rude pencilled score of the will dinner while she tidies the drawing room.
To keep Miss Pruett's personal effects in his own charge until something shows her death was no natural seizure.
To ink out the players' initials in the score-book before any caller sees it, so it no longer shows the vicar was at her surgery so late.
To hide the used tin and Miss Vale's cloak until she can get rid of them, and to put a sealed spare tin on the shelf so nothing looks missing.
To keep out of the investigator's way and Aunt Clara's by spending Friday morning fishing at the boathouse, so nobody asks him about the will dinner.

events.summary: Dorothy closes the post office and balances the day's takings.
Dorothy writes up the parish ledgers at the vestry table.
The vicar works on his sermon in the vestry, then leaves Dorothy at the ledgers.
Silas finishes his letters in his vestry office before walking to the manor.
Ada serves in the bar of the Rook & Lantern.
Ada, hooded in Clara's grey cloak, crosses the square toward the church lane carrying a covered basket.
Ada gives Dorothy hot blackcurrant cordial laced with vermin powder 'for her chest', then leaves.
Ada hangs the grey cloak back on the passage hook and slips behind the bar, serving until closing and after.
Dorothy convulses and dies at the vestry table.
The vicar and Dr Marsh play chess at the surgery.
Dr Marsh tidies her surgery and receives the vicar's telephone call.
The vicar returns to lock up, finds Dorothy dead and telephones for help.
Dr Marsh examines the body and notes signs of strychnine.
Constable Bell walks his round of the square and stays at his house on it.
Constable Bell secures the vestry.
Silas dines at Vale Manor and goes over Edmund's will with the family.
Clara runs the household and hosts dinner at the manor.
Edmund spends the evening at home.
Hugo sits through dinner and the evening at the manor.
Early on Friday, Clara writes Edmund a note asking his silence about the dinner and leaves it on the hall salver.
Edmund reads his sister's note, crumples it and tosses it into the hall wastepaper basket under the salver.
During dinner Hugo pencils times on the back of his menu card, then pushes it under a drawing-room cushion.
Dorothy locks her payment notebook and the Liverpool envelope in the registered-mail safe, then pockets the key.
In the cellar Ada stirs vermin powder into the hot cordial in the flask and leaves the spoon in the tin.
On Friday morning Clara feeds a bundle of moneylender's letters into the morning-room grate and stirs the ashes.
The vicar heads the game in the score-book with its start time. Each player writes their own moves, and he adds the time he resigns.
Ada takes Clara Vale's grey hooded cloak from the passage hooks and puts it on over her apron.
Early on Friday Hugo pulls his scribbled menu card from under the drawing-room cushion and folds it into his blazer's breast pocket.
Early on Friday Dr Marsh inks over the initials heading Thursday's game in the score-book and puts it back on the mantel.
After closing, Ada wraps the used tin in the grey cloak, pushes the bundle behind the cellar barrels and shelves a sealed spare tin.
Hugo takes the boathouse key from the hall board, chalks 'Gone fishing' on the slate and skips breakfast.
Hugo sits at the boathouse with an unused rod and the menu card still folded in his breast pocket.

signs.title: The doctor’s examination notes
signs.text: Examination of the deceased shows a poison taken by mouth. Death was from a poison taken by mouth, and it occurred between twenty-four past nine and quarter to ten.
signs.show: The doctor's notes say the poison was taken by mouth and death occurred between twenty-four past nine and quarter to ten. Does that timing mean anything to you?

reactions.ada: Oh, that poor soul, taken by mouth you say? Dreadful. But I never left my bar all evening, love, so whatever the doctor's found, it's none of my doing.

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Marsh on the body
signs.text: Death was from a poison taken by mouth, and it occurred between twenty-four past nine and quarter to ten.
signs.ask: Doctor, what did you find when you examined Miss Pruett?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says death was from a poison taken by mouth, occurring between twenty-four past nine and quarter to ten. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me death was from a poison taken by mouth, between twenty-four past nine and quarter to ten. Is that your full assessment?

signs.speaker: hugo
signs.title: Hugo Vale on the evening
signs.text: Oh, just the usual dreary business — sat through dinner at the manor being frightfully dull and proper, then hung about the drawing room after. Frightfully thrilling stuff, as you can imagine.
signs.show: Hugo Vale says he simply sat through dinner at the manor and afterward stayed in the drawing room. Do you know if that's the whole of his evening?
signs.confront: You told me you just sat through dinner at the manor and then hung about the drawing room. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: vicar
signs.title: The Reverend Thomas Hale on the evening
signs.text: I sat in the vestry working on my sermon a while, left Miss Pruett to her ledgers, then went along to Dr Marsh's for our usual game of chess. It was only on my return that things took their dreadful turn.
signs.show: The Reverend Hale says he sat in the vestry on his sermon, left Miss Pruett to her ledgers, then went to Dr Marsh's for their usual chess game. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me you worked on your sermon, left Miss Pruett to her ledgers, then went for your usual chess with Dr Marsh. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: edmund
signs.title: Edmund Vale on the evening
signs.text: I dined at home and settled a bit of business with Voss, then sat about the house the rest of the evening. Nothing in it worth the telling.
signs.show: Edmund Vale says he dined at home, settled some business with Voss, and sat about the house the rest of the evening. Do you know if that's accurate?
signs.confront: You told me you dined at home, settled some business with Voss, and sat about the house afterward. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: bell
signs.title: Arthur Bell on the evening
signs.text: I walked my usual round of the square, quiet enough, and looked in on my own house after. Nothing out of the way that I saw, till later.
signs.show: Constable Bell says he walked his usual round of the square and looked in on his own house afterward, seeing nothing out of the way. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me you walked your usual round of the square and then looked in on your own house, nothing out of the way. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on the evening
signs.text: I was at my surgery, tidying up and seeing to a bit of chess, as I do most Thursdays. A perfectly ordinary evening until the telephone rang.
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she was at her surgery tidying up and seeing to a bit of chess, an ordinary evening until the telephone rang. Do you know if that's accurate?
signs.confront: You told me you were at your surgery, tidying up and playing chess, an ordinary evening until the telephone rang. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: ada
signs.title: Ada Finch on the evening
signs.text: Oh, I never stirred from behind the bar, love — you know how it is of an evening, rushed off my feet with the darts crowd in, right up till closing and after. Ask anyone, I'm always there.
signs.show: Ada Finch says she never left the bar all evening, busy with the darts crowd right up till closing. Do you know if that's true?
signs.confront: You told me you never stirred from behind the bar, rushed with the darts crowd till closing. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: silas
signs.title: Silas Voss on the evening
signs.text: I finished my correspondence in the vestry office, then walked up to Vale Manor to dine and go over a small matter of business with the family. A quiet evening, on the whole.
signs.show: Silas Voss says he finished his correspondence in the vestry office, then walked to Vale Manor to dine and discuss business with the family. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me you finished your correspondence at the vestry, then went to Vale Manor to dine and discuss a matter of business. Is that the whole of it?

signs.speaker: clara
signs.title: Clara Vale on the evening
signs.text: I was here at the manor, of course — I saw to the dinner, wrote what letters needed writing, and put the house to rights before I went up. Nothing more remarkable than that.
signs.show: Clara Vale says she was at the manor seeing to dinner, writing letters, and putting the house to rights before going up. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me you saw to the dinner, wrote letters, and put the house to rights before going up. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: Mrs Finch's evening
signs.text: "Left the bar? Me, love? Not for a minute. Thursday's darts night, isn't it, and I was pulling pints from six till gone one. Ask anybody. Poor Dorothy, though. Fancy that, and her so particular about everything."
signs.speaker: ada
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Mrs Finch?
signs.show: Ada Finch says she never left the bar all Thursday night, pulling pints from six till gone one. Do you know if that's true?
signs.confront: You told me you never left the bar, pulling pints from six till gone one. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: Miss Vale's evening
signs.text: "We dined at home. My brother had business with Mr Voss. I cannot think why my evening should interest you, but there it is."
signs.speaker: clara
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Miss Vale?
signs.show: Clara Vale says they dined at home and her brother had business with Mr Voss that evening. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me you dined at home while your brother had business with Mr Voss. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: Mr Voss's evening
signs.text: "I was engaged on a client's affairs, whose I shall not say. Discretion, you understand, is the whole of my trade. Verbum sapienti."
signs.speaker: silas
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Mr Voss?
signs.show: Silas Voss says he was engaged on a client's affairs that evening, but won't say whose. Do you know anything more about that?
signs.confront: You told me you were engaged on a client's affairs but wouldn't say whose. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: Mr Hale's evening
signs.text: "Oh dear. I was at my sermon, then I went out, as I do on Thursdays. Dorothy was at the ledgers when I left. She was always at something, poor soul."
signs.speaker: vicar
signs.ask: Where were you last night, Mr Hale?
signs.show: The Reverend Hale says he worked on his sermon, then went out as he does Thursdays, leaving Miss Pruett at the ledgers. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me you were at your sermon, then went out as usual, leaving Miss Pruett at the ledgers. Is that the whole of it?

signs.title: The Thursday game
signs.text: "Mr Hale came round for our Thursday game, and he stayed until it was finished. He lost, as usual. What time? I don't keep a clock on a game, and I'd rather the village didn't either."
signs.speaker: iris
signs.ask: Did you see anyone last night, Dr Marsh?
signs.reading: The score-book gives the times she won't: the game began at 9.00 and White resigned at 10.30. Every other move is in the vicar's spidery hand, as his sermon notes show, so he sat at the board the whole time.

concede.r_scorebook: Yes, all right — the book says nine to half past ten, and that's what it was; I only kept quiet on the hour because I don't like the village timing Thomas's visits like a train.

signs.show: Dr Marsh says Mr Hale came for their Thursday game and stayed until it finished, though she keeps no clock on it. Do you know if that's accurate?
signs.confront: You told me Mr Hale stayed for the whole game and you keep no clock on it. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.vicar: Well now, Iris never was one for clocks, and I confess I'm much the same when a game's absorbing — Thursday's dragged on rather, as it does, and I couldn't put a time to it myself if you pressed me.

signs.direct: Dr Marsh says you came round for the Thursday game and stayed until it was finished, with no time given. Is that so?

signs.title: Dinner at the manor
signs.text: "My sister? At my table from eight, and in the drawing room till well past eleven. She kept us at it while Voss droned on. Didn't stir."
signs.speaker: edmund
signs.ask: Who was at the manor last night, Mr Vale?
signs.unlock: You put his sister's note in front of Mr Vale, and tell him her cloak was found hidden in the inn cellar. He will not be seen taking orders from Clara, and he is stung that anyone thinks she crept out, so he answers you to show whose house it is.
signs.show: Edmund Vale says his sister was at the table from eight and in the drawing room past eleven, never stirring while Voss talked. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me your sister was at the table from eight and in the drawing room past eleven, and never stirred. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.clara: That is quite correct. My brother kept us all at the table and the drawing room until well past eleven, as I have said, and there is nothing more to add to it.

signs.direct: Mr Vale says you were at his table from eight and in the drawing room till past eleven, and never stirred. Is that so?

signs.title: The will, the whole will
signs.text: "Voss? Droned at Uncle from the soup to the last brandy, and never so much as stepped out for a smoke. Don't ask me for hours, old thing. Aunt Clara would have my head for gossiping about the will."
signs.speaker: hugo
signs.ask: Was Mr Voss at dinner, Mr Hugo?
signs.reading: The card's pencilled times run from 8.00 to 11.20. Hugo's account tells you that 'V.' is Voss, not a Vale, and that he never left the table in between.

concede.i_menu_card: Fine, fine — eight till twenty past eleven, the old menu doesn't lie, and I only ducked the hours because I didn't fancy being the one who put a number on Voss's little chats about the will.

signs.show: Hugo Vale says Mr Voss talked at his uncle from soup to brandy without stepping out, though he won't give exact times. Do you know if that's accurate?
signs.confront: You told me Voss never stepped out all evening, though you wouldn't give exact hours. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.silas: Quite so; the will required careful drafting, and I did not stir from the room. As for hours, festina lente — I was too occupied with clauses to consult my watch.

signs.direct: Mr Hugo says you talked at his uncle from the soup through to the last brandy and never stepped out. Is that so?

signs.title: On the round
signs.text: "Walked my round of the square from nine. About twenty past, a woman in a grey hooded cloak came across from the inn corner with a covered basket and went up the church lane. Miss Vale, I took it to be. That's her church cloak, see. Thought nothing of it at the time."
signs.speaker: bell
signs.unlock: Once Mrs Finch swears she never left the bar, you ask Constable Bell, who walks his round of the square between the inn and the church lane every night.
signs.ask: Mr Bell, what can you tell me about your evening on the round?
signs.confront: Constable Bell says he saw a woman in a grey hooded cloak, with a covered basket, cross to the church lane around twenty past nine, and he took her for you. Was that you?

reactions.clara: A grey hooded cloak, church lane, twenty past nine — yes, that would be mine, kept on the passage hook for anyone to take up. I was in the drawing room at the time, so it was evidently not I who wore it.

signs.direct: Constable Bell says he saw a woman in your grey hooded cloak go up the church lane about twenty past nine with a covered basket, and took her for you. Is that so?
signs.show: Constable Bell says that around twenty past nine he saw a woman in a grey hooded cloak, who he took for Miss Vale, crossing to the church lane. Does that match what you saw?

signs.title: The master is not at home to questions
signs.text: Mr Vale draws himself up, filling the space before him. "Thursday? Dined, went to bed. What my family does at my table is nobody's affair, least of all a stranger's." He glances once to the side and sets his jaw, closing the subject.
signs.show: Mr Vale refused to say what his family did at his table on Thursday, glancing toward the hall before shutting the door. Do you know why he was so unwilling to speak of it?
signs.confront: You glanced toward the hall and shut the door rather than say what your family did at your table on Thursday. Is there something you're not telling me?

reactions.edmund: That's the whole of it. My table, my house, my business — I'll not have a stranger poking into what my family says over dinner.

signs.direct: You stood in your doorway, said only that you dined and went to bed, glanced toward the hall, and shut the door on me. Is there more you'd care to tell me?

signs.title: A crumpled note in the hall basket
signs.text: A sheet of manor notepaper, screwed into a ball, lies in the wastepaper basket under the hall salver. Smoothed out, it reads in a neat, narrow hand: "E. — Please say nothing to anyone about last night: not the dinner, not Mr Voss, not the will. The village talks enough. C."
signs.unlock: Before he shut the door Mr Vale glanced toward the hall, so you go and look there. Under the salver is the wastepaper basket, and a fresh ball of notepaper lies on top.
signs.show: A crumpled note found in the manor hall basket asks someone called E. to say nothing about the dinner, Mr Voss, or the will, signed C. Do you know anything about this?

reactions.clara: Yes, I wrote that. A family dislikes gossip about a will, Inspector, and I see no crime in asking my brother to hold his tongue.

signs.direct: You wrote this note asking E. to say nothing about last night, the dinner, Mr Voss, or the will. Why did you need it kept quiet?

signs.title: A menu card in a breast pocket
signs.text: A folded Vale Manor dinner menu card from Thursday. On the back, in hurried pencil: "8.00 V. arr. Soup." "9.40 Codicil the third. V. still here." "10.30 V. hasn't moved. Nor has Uncle." "11.20 V. STILL at it. Send help."
signs.unlock: You ask Mr Hugo what he keeps patting. Caught out, and more afraid of looking a liar than of his aunt, he pulls the folded card out of his pocket and hands it over, begging you not to show Aunt Clara.
signs.show: A dinner menu card found in a breast pocket has pencilled times noting Voss's continued presence right through to half past eleven. Do you know anything about this card?

reactions.hugo: Ha — caught red-handed being frightfully bored, that's all. Poor old Voss did go on rather, didn't he? I only scribbled it to stop myself screaming, not because anything sinister was happening.

signs.title: The postmistress's keys
signs.text: Constable Bell hands over the key ring he took from Miss Pruett's coat at the vestry. On it are a church key, a latchkey and a small brass key stamped 'G.P.O. — REG.'
signs.unlock: Constable Bell keeps Miss Pruett's effects under lock and puts the bitter dregs down to cordial gone off. Once you show him the hidden strychnine tin with its purple-stained spoon, he agrees this was no natural fit and hands you the key ring taken from her coat.
signs.show: Constable Bell handed over a key ring taken from Miss Pruett's coat, including a small brass key stamped for registered mail. Do you know anything about these keys?
signs.direct: This key ring, with your church key, latchkey, and Post Office key, was found in your coat at the vestry. Can you tell me about it?

signs.title: Inside the registered-mail safe
signs.text: Under the sheets of stamps lies a small black notebook. In a prim hand: '1 Aug — A.F. — £5.' '1 Sept — A.F. — £5.' '1 Oct — A.F. — £5 (late).' Tucked inside is an envelope postmarked Liverpool and addressed to Mrs A. Finch, the Rook & Lantern. Its flap is cockled and has been stuck down again.
signs.unlock: The brass key stamped 'REG.' fits the registered-mail safe behind the post office counter, and only the postmistress carried it.
signs.show: A notebook in the registered-mail safe records monthly five-pound payments from A.F., alongside an opened envelope addressed to Mrs Finch at the Rook and Lantern. Do you know anything about these payments?

reactions.ada: Oh, that. Well, love, a woman's private letters are her own affair, aren't they — and paying a bit here and there is hardly a hanging matter, whatever Dorothy made of it.

signs.title: The flask by the ledgers
signs.text: A blue enamel flask stands by the ledgers with a purple rime of blackcurrant dregs inside. They smell sharply bitter. Painted small on the base are the letters 'R & L'.
signs.show: A blue enamel flask by the ledgers holds a sharply bitter purple residue and is marked 'R & L'. Do you know anything about this flask?

signs.title: A bundle behind the barrels
signs.text: Inside the bundled cloak behind the ale barrels is a tin of rat powder labelled 'Contains Strychnine'. The lid sits loose. A teaspoon is pushed down into the powder, and its bowl is stained a dark purple. Its base fits the ring in the shelf dust exactly.
signs.unlock: The gravel leads from the empty hook to the cellar door, and the ring in the dust shows that a bigger tin once stood on the shelf. So you search the cellar and pull a bundle out from behind the ale barrels.
signs.reading: Strychnine is intensely bitter, like the dregs in the flask. The purple stain on the spoon matches the blackcurrant cordial, so the powder was stirred in from this tin.
signs.show: A tin of strychnine rat powder was found in a bundled cloak behind the ale barrels, with a purple-stained teaspoon pressed into it that matches a ring in the shelf dust. Do you know anything about this?

reactions.ada: That's just the rat powder we keep for the cellar, love, everyone knows mice get into the barrels. As for the spoon, I couldn't tell you how that got left in there, honest.

signs.title: Miss Vale at the grate
signs.text: You are shown into the morning room at a quarter past eight. Miss Vale is kneeling at the grate with the poker, though it is a mild morning. The room smells of burnt paper. She stands at once, sets the poker down and draws the fire-screen across. "You are early," she says.
signs.show: Miss Vale was found kneeling at the grate with the poker on a mild morning, the room smelling of burnt paper, and she stood at once to screen the fire. Do you know what she might have been burning?
signs.confront: You were kneeling at the grate with the poker on a mild morning, and the room smelled of burnt paper. What were you burning?

reactions.clara: You are, rather. A woman may tidy her own grate on a mild morning without it being made a matter for the police, surely.

signs.direct: I found you kneeling at the grate with a poker on a mild morning, the room smelling of burnt paper, and you quickly put the poker down and drew the screen across. What were you burning?

signs.title: A scrap in the ashes
signs.text: A brown-edged corner of letter paper lies in the ash behind the fire-screen. Printed heading: 'Gribble & Stone, Advances Arranged, Holborn.' Typed below: '...Mr E. Vale ... the sum of £1,200 remains outstanding ... final notice before proceedings...' It is dated the 14th of September.
signs.unlock: Having seen Miss Vale pull the screen across the grate, you look behind it when she goes out of the room to ring for the maid.
signs.show: A scrap of burnt letter paper found behind the fire-screen is from a lending firm, naming Mr E. Vale over an outstanding twelve hundred pounds with proceedings threatened. Do you know anything about this?

reactions.clara: My brother's affairs, and none of yours nor the village's. I burned it because Edmund would not wish his troubles read out over every counter in the parish, and I still don't.

signs.direct: This burnt letter from Gribble & Stone demands £1,200 outstanding from you, dated the 14th of September. Can you tell me about this debt?

signs.title: The chess score-book
signs.text: A cloth-bound chess score-book lies on the surgery mantel. The last entry is headed 'Thurs. Commenced 9.0 p.m.', and after that comes a fresh, glossy smear of ink where two sets of initials were written. Forty-one moves follow, and the hand changes with every move: one spidery with looped descenders, the other brisk and upright. At the foot, in the spidery hand: 'White resigns, 10.30 p.m.'
signs.reading: The spidery hand with its looped descenders matches Mr Hale's sermon draft. The vicar wrote every other move, so he was at this board from 9.00 until he resigned at 10.30.

reactions.vicar: Ah — forty-one moves, was it, I always did play too long into the endgame. Iris and I simply enjoy our chess without watching the hour, and I fear the ink got smudged in the pushing about of things afterward.
reactions.iris: Yes, we played our usual Thursday game, and I'm afraid I did smear the initials myself before tidying the mantel — I'd rather the village not chatter about how late the vicar sits in my surgery, that's the whole of it.

signs.show: There's a chess score-book on the surgery mantel, its last game begun at nine and finished at half past ten, with two sets of initials smeared away before the moves. Can you tell me who was playing that game?

signs.title: A cloak behind the barrels
signs.text: Pushed behind the ale barrels in the inn cellar is a bundled grey hooded cloak of good wool. The hem is damp and flecked with gravel. There is a small purple splash dried stiff on the right cuff. A tape sewn inside the collar reads 'C. VALE'.
signs.unlock: The gravel leads from the empty lost-property hook to the cellar door, and the ring in the shelf dust shows that something was moved. So you search behind the ale barrels.
signs.show: A grey hooded cloak was found bundled behind the ale barrels, damp at the hem, with a purple splash on the cuff and a collar tape reading 'C. VALE'. Do you know how it came to be there?

reactions.ada: That old grey cloak? Miss Vale must've left it hanging in our passage some time, and heaven knows how a splash got on it, love — I certainly never wore the thing.

signs.direct: This grey hooded cloak, marked 'C. VALE' inside the collar, was found behind the ale barrels with a damp hem and a purple splash on the cuff. Can you explain that?

signs.title: Second thoughts on the round
signs.text: "Stuffed behind the barrels at the inn, was it? Then I've been a proper fool. Miss Vale's tall and walks like a guardsman. The one I saw was short, round and quick on her feet, and she came out of the inn yard, not down the manor road. That was Mrs Finch in that cloak. I'd stake my helmet on it."
signs.speaker: bell
signs.ask: Could the woman in the cloak have been someone other than Miss Vale, Constable?
signs.unlock: You take the grey cloak you found behind the inn's cellar barrels to Constable Bell and ask him to think again about the figure he saw.
signs.show: Constable Bell now says the woman he saw was short and quick, coming from the inn yard rather than the manor road, and he now believes it was Mrs Finch, not Miss Vale. Do you know anything about that?
signs.confront: You're now saying the woman you saw was short and quick, coming from the inn yard, and that it was Mrs Finch, not Miss Vale. Are you certain of that?

reactions.ada: Now, now, love, a man can mistake a shape in the dark easy enough, and I told you plain I never left my bar all night. Whatever Arthur thinks he saw, it wasn't me stuffing anything behind any barrels.

signs.direct: Constable Bell now says the woman he saw in that cloak was short, round and quick, out of the inn yard, and he believes it was you. Is that so?

signs.title: Mr Hugo's breast pocket
signs.text: Mr Hugo holds a fishing rod he isn't using, all jokes. Each time dinner comes up, his hand goes to the breast pocket of his blazer and pats it flat. When you look at the pocket he stops, laughs too loudly and puts his hands behind his back.
signs.unlock: The empty 'Boathouse' hook and the chalked 'Gone fishing. H.' send you down the river path to the boathouse, where Mr Hugo has gone to ground.
signs.show: Mr Hugo keeps patting his breast pocket whenever dinner comes up, then stops and laughs too loudly when he notices you looking. Do you know what he's keeping in there?
signs.confront: Every time dinner comes up, you pat your breast pocket, then stop and laugh when I look at it. What's in there?

reactions.hugo: This? Oh, just — er — fishing tackle receipts, frightfully thrilling stuff. Nothing to do with dinner at all, I promise you, I'm just a chap who likes his pocket tidy.

signs.direct: Each time dinner comes up, your hand goes to your breast pocket, and you stop and laugh too loudly when you catch me looking. What is it you're carrying there?

signs.title: Pencilled sheets on the vestry desk
signs.text: On the vicar's side of the vestry desk lie several sheets of a sermon draft on Luke xiv. The hand is thin and spidery, with long looped descenders and a crossed 7. In the margin: 'Ask T.H. to find the Tertullian. T.H.' (a note to himself).
signs.show: Sermon sheets on the vestry desk are written in a thin, spidery hand with looped descenders and a crossed seven, with a note to himself signed T.H. Do you know anything about these sheets?

reactions.vicar: Ah yes, my little reminder to myself about the Tertullian — one does talk to oneself rather, in sermon-writing, T.H. to T.H. as it were, no mystery in that at all.

signs.title: A sealed tin on the cellar shelf
signs.text: On a shelf in the inn cellar stands a tin of rat powder labelled 'Contains Strychnine'. Its paper seal is unbroken and the lid is tight. Beside it is a paler ring in the dust, a good deal wider than this tin's base.
signs.unlock: The flask carries the Rook & Lantern's mark, so Constable Bell takes you down to the inn cellar, where the stores are kept, while the bar is busy.
signs.show: A sealed tin of strychnine rat powder sits untouched on the inn cellar shelf, beside a paler ring in the dust much wider than the tin itself. Do you know what usually stood in that wider ring?

reactions.ada: Oh, that? That's just the spare, love, seal's not even broke on it — I always keep one by in case we run short. Rats in a cellar, what can you do, you can't leave the shelf bare. Wider ring in the dust? Lor', I couldn't tell you, I'm not one for staring at dust of an evening.

signs.title: An empty hook in the passage
signs.text: On the inn's passage hooks hang a barman's coat, two mackintoshes and a cap. Above the last hook is a hand-lettered card: 'Left at Harvest Supper, please ask at bar.' That hook is empty. On the flagstones below lie a few grains of gravel, and a few more lead to the cellar door.
signs.unlock: Constable Bell said the cloaked woman came from the inn corner, so you look along the inn's passage hooks, where customers and staff hang their coats.
signs.show: One hook in the inn passage, marked for an item left at the Harvest Supper, is empty, with gravel grains on the flagstones leading toward the cellar door. Do you know what was on that hook?

reactions.ada: That's Miss Vale's old grey cloak, love, left over from the Harvest Supper — I keep meaning to send it round to her. Gravel? Must've come off someone's boots, we get all sorts traipsing through of an evening. I never touched it myself, I was behind the bar the whole time, as I said.

signs.title: An empty hook in the manor hall
signs.text: In the manor hall hangs a board of keys on hooks, each with a painted label. The hook marked 'Boathouse' is empty. On the slate beneath it someone has chalked: 'Gone fishing. Don't wait luncheon. H.' In the dining room one breakfast place is still laid, and nobody has touched it.
signs.show: The boathouse key is missing from its hook in the manor hall, and a chalked note says 'Gone fishing,' though one breakfast place remains untouched. Do you know where that key or its owner might be?

reactions.hugo: Ha, guilty as charged — thought I'd rather face a pike than another word about codicils, so I scarpered before anyone could pin me down over toast. Slate's not lying, that's my hand, my rotten spelling and all. Nothing sinister, just a chap avoiding the third degree over kippers.

signs.direct: The Boathouse key is gone from its hook, and you left word on the slate that you'd gone fishing and not to wait luncheon. Where did you go?

signs.title: The letter inside the Liverpool envelope
signs.text: A single folded sheet inside the resealed Liverpool envelope reads: "Ada, I'm writing because you ought to know your husband is alive and living here in Liverpool, whatever you've let them believe down there. You're no widow, and it's not right you should go on calling yourself one. I'll say no more on paper."
signs.unlock: once you have inside the registered-mail safe, you know what to ask
signs.show: A letter sent to Ada through a Liverpool envelope tells her that her husband is alive and living there, and that she's no widow. Did you know anything about this?
signs.direct: This letter tells you your husband is alive in Liverpool, though you've let everyone believe you're a widow. Is that true?

signs.title: When it happened
signs.text: Dorothy Pruett died between 21:24 and 21:45.

signs.title: Who had Tin of vermin powder
signs.text: Only Ada Finch had Tin of vermin powder.

synopsis: Dorothy Pruett was found dead at St. Alden’s vestry.

clara: I keep house at Vale Manor, seeing to the meals, the linens, and the staff's work each day.
I am Edmund Vale's younger sister, and I have run this household for years.
I live at the manor, where I keep my own things in my rooms and see to the running of the whole house.
I know Dr Marsh, the vicar, and Mr Voss through village life and the manor's dealings with the church and the law.
I understand poor Miss Pruett was found this morning and that word was sent for Dr Marsh and Constable Bell straightaway.
rowan: I am the manor's groundskeeper, and my days are spent among the glasshouses and the grounds.
I live in the greenhouse and keep my tools and seed-boxes there.
I know the Vale family and the manor staff from my years of work on the grounds.
I don't have much cause to go into the village proper, keeping mostly to my plants.
silas: I am the village solicitor, and I keep an office in the vestry where I handle papers for half the parish.
I know the vicar well, sharing the vestry building with him, and I know Mr Vale through his affairs.
I hold a key to the vestry office, as is proper for a man who keeps papers there.
ada: I keep the Rook & Lantern, pulling pints and keeping the bar of an evening.
I know most everyone in the village, since they all pass through my inn sooner or later.
iris: I know the vicar well, as we are both from the same circle of village society.
I was sent for this morning when Miss Pruett was found, as is usual when someone dies suddenly.
bell: I am the village constable, and I keep my rounds and see to order in the village.
I live near the square, where I can be found most days.
I know everyone in the village through my duties, from the manor to the inn to the post office.
I am holding Miss Pruett's personal effects in my own charge for now, as is proper until we know more.
edmund: I live at the manor, where I keep my study, my papers, and my own rooms.
I know Mr Voss as my solicitor, who has long handled the family's affairs.
vicar: I am vicar of St. Alden's, and I tend to the parish, the church, and its people.
I live at the vestry, where I keep my books, my sermons, and my own rooms.
I know Mr Voss well, sharing the vestry building with him for his office.
jonah: I keep the manor's boathouse and serve as ferryman when the river runs high.
I live at the boathouse, where I keep the boats, the oars, and my own gear.
I know the Vale family, since I look after their boats and the river crossing for them.
I hold a key to the boathouse, being its keeper, though others at the manor have one too for their own use.
hugo: I am Edmund's nephew, down from London, and I've been staying at the manor a while now.
I live at the manor while I'm here, keeping my things in my room there.
I know Aunt Clara and Uncle Edmund as family, and I've come to know the village a little through them.
I know Mr Voss a little, as he sees to my uncle's affairs.

moods.rowan: Quiet and steady, going about his usual work in the grounds with nothing on his mind.
moods.silas: Formal and a little guarded, keen to bury himself in paperwork rather than talk.
moods.ada: Busy and cheerful behind the bar, tired from the day's trade but otherwise untroubled.
moods.iris: Brisk and professional, but oddly eager to tidy her own records before anyone else looks at them.
moods.bell: Alert and a touch pompous, treating the morning as official business and guarding what's been left in his charge.
moods.edmund: Absent this morning, his household left to manage without him.
moods.vicar: Stiff and irritable, short with anyone who pries into parish letters or his own comings and goings.
moods.jonah: Calm and unhurried, tending the boathouse as any ordinary morning.
